newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yeltsin, Japan PM to meet - diplomatic source.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Japan PM to meet - diplomatic source.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will visit Russia in early November for talks with President Boris Yeltsin aimed at improving frosty bilateral relations, a diplomatic source said on Tuesday.

Hashimoto's visit may showcase efforts by both sides towards a wide-ranging thaw that has been hampered by a bitter territorial dispute dating back to World War Two, said the source, who did not want to be otherwise identified.
The meeting may take place at Yeltsin's villa near Lake Baikal in Siberia, the source said.
"It would probably be a no-necktie type of meeting, something along the lines of a similar meeting at the villa between Yeltsin and (German Chancellor Helmut) Kohl in 1993," the source said.
Japanese Foreign Ministry officials said the date for Hashimoto's visit was not fixed and that the Baikal venue was one of several options. The Russian Far East port of Vladivostok was another.
Last month, Hashimoto announced a new policy for improving ties with Russia, based on "mutual trust, mutual benefit and long-term goals".
Hashimoto's announcement marked a departure from Japan's traditional policy of placing top priority on a political solution to a dispute over Russian-held islands claimed by Japan.

The Soviet army seized the islands, known as the Northern Territories in Japan and Southern Kuriles by Russia, in the last days of World War Two. The row over ownership has prevented the countries signing a World War Two peace treaty.

Until Hashimoto's July 25 policy change, successive Japanese governments had said there would be no expansion of economic ties -- meaning aid or large-scale investment in Russia -- without a political solution to the islands dispute.
"The solution to the territorial problem should not be sought on the basis of one side winning and the other losing," Hashimoto said in a speech announcing Japan's new Russia policy.

In May, the Russian defence minister visited Japan and said he welcomed stronger defence ties between the United States and Japan, a comment that had seemed unthinkable even after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
For its part, Japan has stopped calling Russia a latent military threat, the key Cold War phrase used to justify its military buildup under the U.S.-Japan security arrangement.
